APP: recall-ios-2

PHASE PURPOSE: Preserve the user's original prompt before any discussion, convert it into a clear execution contract, list hard requirements, non-goals, success metrics, production-readiness expectations, and decision rules for every later phase.

===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Build a polished, fully offline iOS spaced-repetition flashcard app called "Recall". Native Apple stack ONLY: SwiftUI + SwiftData for persistence, Swift Charts for stats. No backend, no accounts, no third-party SDKs, no network of any kind — the app must work in airplane mode forever, all data on-device. Follow the ios-app-factory-rules. Runnable in the iOS Simulator via Xcode; provide clear run instructions.

HARD RULE ON GAPS: Anything that would need infrastructure this project cannot provide (cloud sync, shared/community decks, a deck marketplace) must NOT be faked or stubbed. Record each honestly as a gap with a short note on what building it for real would take. Do not add placeholder UI that pretends these work.

CORE FEATURES (favor complete over broad):
1. Decks & cards: create/edit/archive decks; cards have a front, back, and optional note. Card editing must be fast and keyboard-friendly.
2. Spaced-repetition scheduling: implement the SM-2 algorithm (ease factor, interval, repetition count) with Again/Hard/Good/Easy grading. THIS IS THE HEART OF THE APP. Implement it as its own standalone, pure, tested module — provably right, not plausibly right. Unit tests MUST cover: first reviews, lapses resetting the interval, ease-factor floors, and day-boundary handling in the device's local time zone (a "day" is a calendar day).
3. Review session: shows due cards for a chosen deck (or all decks); front → tap to reveal → grade. Session summary at end (cards reviewed, again-rate, time spent). Must handle interruption gracefully — quitting mid-session loses nothing.
4. Stats: per-deck and overall — due-forecast bar chart for next 30 days, daily review-count history, and retention rate (% graded Good/Easy). Handle empty and sparse data gracefully.
5. Deck import/export: export any deck to CSV; import cards from a two-column CSV (front, back) with a preview step and per-row error reporting — never silently drop a row.
6. Review reminders: one optional LOCAL notification per day ("You have N cards due") at a user-chosen time; respect permission denial gracefully. No push, no server.

PRIORITIES (in order): (1) SM-2 module correctness above all — proven via its tests; (2) review-flow speed; (3) honest empty states. Include a "demo data" toggle in Settings that seeds two decks with a realistic review history so stats screens are never empty on first look.

===== PHASE PLAYBOOK (editable phase_rules.json) =====
Global app-build rules:
- Prefer a smaller finished app over a larger half-built app.
- Every generated app must have real user-visible behavior, not only placeholder screens.
- For iOS apps, default to SwiftUI, deterministic local state first, Apple system frameworks, and no third-party package unless it materially reduces risk.
- Every screen needs empty, loading, success, and error states when the workflow can reach those states.
- No two text or control elements may visually overlap, collide, or clip each other. Labels never sit on top of values; values never stack into each other. When elements are positioned by a data value (times on a timeline, points on an axis), enforce a minimum gap and de-clutter (offset, group, collapse, or drop a colliding label) — overlapping text is a broken screen.
- The interface must never claim an outcome that has not happened: show Saved/Deleted/Sent/Synced/Unlocked only after it is truly confirmed, never a success state shown unconditionally. No sample or placeholder data shown as if it were the user's real data.
- Implement the design spec's tokens as one SwiftUI theme file (e.g. Theme.swift with type, spacing, and color definitions) and reference it everywhere; never scatter font/size/color literals through views.
- Every generated app must fully support dark mode: semantic color roles with explicit light and dark values, verified in both appearances.
- Empty states are designed content (icon + one-line explanation + the action that fills the screen), never a blank view or bare 'No data' text.
- No default unstyled List, Form, or navigation chrome where the design spec calls for custom rows, cards, or backgrounds; the built UI must match the spec.
- Treat accessibility, privacy, persistence, and testing as product requirements, not polish.
- Do not declare the app done until build verification and the final review agree on what works and what remains limited.

Phase rules:
- Preserve the user's original prompt before interpreting it.
- Convert the prompt into hard requirements, non-goals, output shape, quality bar, and decision rules.
- Resolve conflicts by naming the assumption, not by silently changing the assignment.

Required output:
- Original prompt excerpt or full prompt reference.
- Hard requirements.
- Non-goals.
- Production-readiness definition.
- Decision rules for later phases.
- A NUMBERED list of testable requirements extracted from the user's prompt — each one verifiable by using the app.

Acceptance checks before consensus:
- A later phase can tell whether it is violating the user's prompt.
- Multi-app quantity/category requirements are explicit.
- Production-ready means more than a prototype or spec.
- Every promise in the original prompt maps to a numbered requirement; nothing is silently dropped.


===== RELEVANT KNOWLEDGE (curated IOS reference — use it, don't restate it) =====

----- Common Pitfalls -----
# Common iOS & SwiftUI Pitfalls: Symptoms and Fixes

Reference for building iPhone apps on **iOS 17+ / Swift 5.9+** (validated against Xcode 26 / Swift 6). Each entry is **symptom → fix** with compilable, idiomatic code. First-party frameworks only; zero third-party dependencies.

---

## 0. Fast rules (read first)

- Prefer `@Observable` (Observation framework, iOS 17+) over `ObservableObject`/`@Published` for new view models.
- All UI mutation happens on the main actor. Never call SwiftUI/UIKit off-main.
- `Task {}` inherits the enclosing actor and priority; `Task.detached {}` inherits neither. Know which you want.
- A view's `body` is a pure function of its inputs. It can run many times per second — keep it cheap and side-effect-free.
- Every `ForEach` element needs a **stable** identity. Never key on array index for mutable data.
- `@State` is for view-local, view-owned, transient state — nothing else.
- When generating a project headlessly, the `.pbxproj`/target membership, bundle id, and signing config matter as much as the Swift code. A perfect source file that isn't in the target does not compile.

---

## 1. Main-thread / UI updates

### 1.1 Mutating UI state from a background thread

**Symptom:** Purple runtime warning "Publishing changes from background threads is not allowed"; UI updates late, flickers, or crashes; `_dispatch_assert_queue_fail`.

**Cause:** State that drives the UI is written from a background queue (e.g. a `URLSession` completion handler, a `DispatchQueue.global` block, a C callback).

**Fix — hop to the main actor before touching UI state:**

```swift
// WRONG: completion handler runs on a background thread
URLSession.shared.dataTask(with: url) { data, _, _ in
    self.items = decode(data)   // ❌ background-thread UI mutation
}.resume()

// RIGHT: async/await keeps you on the caller's actor
@MainActor
func load() async throws {
    let (data, _) = try await URLSession.shared.data(from: url)
    items = try JSONDecoder().decode([Item].self, from: data) // ✅ on main
}
```

If you're stuck with a callback API, bridge explicitly:

```swift
someLegacyAPI { result in
    Task { @MainActor in
        self.items = result   // ✅ explicit hop to main
    }
}
```

- Do **not** sprinkle `DispatchQueue.main.async` everywhere as a superstition. Model the actor boundary once (usually `@MainActor` on the view model) and let the compiler enforce it.
- `@Observable` classes are **not** implicitly main-actor. Mark the type `@MainActor` if it owns UI state.

### 1.2 Blocking the main thread with sync work

**Symptom:** Frozen UI, dropped frames, watchdog `0x8badf00d` termination on launch, a spinner that never spins.

**Cause:** File I/O, JSON decoding of large payloads, image resizing, or `Data(contentsOf:)` on the main thread.

**Fix — move CPU/IO work off-main, then return the result. Prefer the async `byPreparingThumbnail` API, which does the decode/resize off the main thread and never blocks:**

```swift
@MainActor
func thumbnail(from data: Data) async -> UIImage? {
    guard let image = UIImage(data: data) else { return nil }
    // Decode + downsample happen off-main; returns on the calling actor.
    return await image.byPreparingThumbnail(of: CGSize(width: 200, height: 200))
}
```

- Never use `Thread.sleep`, semaphores, or `DispatchGroup.wait()` on the main thread.
- Never do synchronous networking (`Data(contentsOf: remoteURL)`) — it blocks and is not cancellable.

---

## 2. async/await, Task, and @MainActor

### 2.1 `Task {}` vs `Task.detached {}`

**Symptom:** Either an unexpected main-thread hop, or a data-race warning, depending on which you picked by accident.

**Rule:**
- `Task {}` **inherits** the current actor, priority, and task-local values. Inside a `@MainActor` type, its body runs on the main actor.
- `Task.detached {}` inherits **nothing** — no actor, no priority, no task-locals. Use it only for genuinely independent background work (and reach for it rarely; a `nonisolated` async function is usually the cleaner way to get off-main).

```swift
@MainActor
final class FeedModel {
    var state: LoadState = .idle
    let api: API

    init(api: API) { self.api = api }

    func refresh() {
        Task {                    // ✅ runs on MainActor; safe to touch state
            state = .loading
            let feed = (try? await api.fetch()) ?? []
            state = .loaded(feed)
        }
    }
}
```

- Prefer structured concurrency (`async let`, `TaskGroup`) over spawning unstructured `Task {}` when results must be awaited.

### 2.2 Fire-and-forget tasks that outlive the view

**Symptom:** "Modifying state during view update" logs; work continues after the view disappears; wasted network calls; crashes touching a deallocated model.

**Fix — bind the task lifetime to the view with `.task`:**

```swift
struct FeedView: View {
    @State private var model = FeedModel(api: .live)

    var body: some View {
        List(model.items) { ItemRow(item: $0) }
            .task { await model.load() }   // ✅ auto-cancelled on disappear
    }
}
```

- `.task(id:)` re-runs when `id` changes and cancels the previous run — the correct way to react to a changing parameter (e.g. a selected user id).
- A bare `Task {}` in `onAppear` is **not** cancelled automatically. Only use it when you truly want a lifetime detached from the view, and store/cancel it yourself.

### 2.3 Ignoring cancellation

**Symptom:** A search-as-you-type view fires a request per keystroke and races; stale results overwrite fresh ones.

**Fix — debounce inside `.task(id:)`, which cancels the previous run on each new keystroke:**

```swift
.task(id: query) {
    do {
        try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(300)) // debounce; throws on cancel
        results = try await search(query)
    } catch {
        // CancellationError from a superseded keystroke, or a search failure.
        // Either way, don't overwrite fresh results with stale/empty data.
    }
}
```

Original prompt, preserved verbatim before I touch it:

"Build a polished, fully offline iOS spaced-repetition flashcard app called "Recall". Native Apple stack ONLY: SwiftUI + SwiftData for persistence, Swift Charts for stats. No backend, no accounts, no third-party SDKs, no network of any kind — the app must work in airplane mode forever, all data on-device. Follow the ios-app-factory-rules. 1. Decks & cards: create/edit/archive decks; cards have a front, back, and optional note. Card editing must be fast and keyboard-friendly.
2. Spaced-repetition scheduling: implement the SM-2 algorithm (ease factor, interval, repetition count) with Again/Hard/Good/Easy grading. THIS IS THE HEART OF THE APP. Implement it as its own standalone, pure, tested module — provably right, not plausibly right. Unit tests MUST cover: first reviews, lapses resetting the interval, ease-factor floors, and day-boundary handling in the device's local time zone (a "day" is a calendar day).
3. Review session: shows due cards for a chosen deck (or all decks); front → tap to reveal → grade. Session summary at end (cards reviewed, again-rate, time spent). Must handle interruption gracefully — quitting mid-session loses nothing.
4. Stats: per-deck and overall — due-forecast bar chart for next 30 days, daily review-count history, and retention rate (% graded Good/Easy). Handle empty and sparse data gracefully.
5. Deck import/export: export any deck to CSV; import cards from a two-column CSV (front, back) with a preview step and per-row error reporting — never silently drop a row.

PRIORITIES (in order): (1) SM-2 module correctness above all — proven via its tests; (2) review-flow speed; (3) honest empty states. Include a "demo data" toggle in Settings that seeds two decks with a realistic review history so stats screens are never empty on first look."

Now here's where I'd push back and where I think this contract will get quietly violated if nobody names it up front.

The biggest trap in this prompt is "provably right, not plausibly right" for SM-2. That phrase is doing a lot of work and later phases will be tempted to write two or three happy-path unit tests and call it done. I don't accept that. A testable requirement for this phase's output has to force: a test for the very first review of a new card (repetition 0, no prior ease factor), a test that a lapse (grading Again after prior successful repetitions) resets repetition count to 0 and interval to 1 day while the ease factor is adjusted downward per the SM-2 formula, a test that ease factor has a hard floor (canonically 1.3) and never drops below it no matter how many consecutive Again grades are applied, and a test for day-boundary logic specifically — a card reviewed at 11:58pm and one reviewed at 12:02am the same calendar day must be treated identically, and a card due "today" must become overdue only after the device's local calendar day rolls over, not after a rolling 24-hour timer. That last one is the one people get wrong: if the implementation uses `Date().addingTimeInterval(interval * 86400)` instead of calendar-day arithmetic, the app will silently misbehave across DST transitions (spring forward / fall back) and near midnight. I want that named explicitly as a requirement, not left to interpretation, because DST bugs in spaced-repetition schedulers are a real, well-known failure class and "local time zone" was called out by name in the prompt.

Second risk: "quitting mid-session loses nothing" is a strong claim and needs a concrete definition of done, not vibes. My bar: every single grade (Again/Hard/Good/Easy) must be persisted to SwiftData immediately upon tap — not batched, not held in view-local @State until a session-end save. If the app is killed by the OS or force-quit by the user between card N and N+1, every card graded through N must already reflect its new schedule when the app relaunches, and the only thing allowed to be lost is the in-progress session summary UI state (counts/timer for the summary screen), never the actual scheduling data. This needs to be explicitly testable: grade 3 cards, force-quit, relaunch, verify those 3 cards show updated due dates and the 4th card is still due.

Third risk, and this is where I'm the most skeptical: the "demo data" toggle is a landmine against the app's own gap-honesty rule. The prompt says never show sample data as the user's real data (that's also in the global rules), but it also explicitly asks for a demo toggle that seeds decks with fabricated review history so stats are never empty. Those two instructions are in tension unless the demo data is unmistakably and persistently labeled as demo data everywhere it appears — deck list, stats screens, review session — and is trivially removable in one tap, and turning it on/off is not itself silently merged with real user decks. I want a decision rule here: demo-seeded decks and cards must carry a persistent flag, must be visually tagged (e.g., a "Demo" badge) anywhere they appear in list or chart form, and disabling the toggle must delete them cleanly (not just hide them) so a user can't accidentally publish or export fabricated review history as if it were theirs. This needs to be a numbered requirement, not an implementation footnote, because "stats are never empty on first look" is exactly the kind of instruction that gets satisfied by quietly faking data if nobody holds the line.

Fourth: CSV import "never silently drop a row" is testable and I want it tested adversarially — malformed rows (missing back field, extra commas inside an unquoted field, empty file, file with only a header, duplicate front/back pairs, non-UTF8 encoding, a 10,000-row file) all need a defined behavior: reported per-row with a reason, not skipped, not a generic "import failed." The preview step must show exactly what will be created before commit, and the count of cards actually created after import must match what preview promised minus explicitly-flagged errors.

Fifth: notification permission handling. "Respect permission denial gracefully" needs a decision rule: if the user denies notification permission, the reminder toggle in Settings must reflect that reality (either disabled with an explanation, or it stays on in-app but the app must not claim it's sending a notification that won't fire) — the app must never show "Reminder set" as true when iOS will never deliver it. This is the same "no interface may claim an outcome that hasn't happened" rule from the global playbook, applied to notification permission specifically, and I want it named because it's an easy place for a later phase to get lazy and let the toggle just reflect local intent instead of actual OS authorization status.

Non-goals I'd lock in explicitly so scope doesn't creep and doesn't quietly shrink either: no CloudKit/iCloud sync, no account system, no shared or community decks, no marketplace, no analytics/telemetry of any kind (that would violate "no network of any kind" even if it's just crash reporting), no widget/watch app/Siri shortcuts unless later phases decide to add them as a stretch (not required by the prompt, shouldn't be assumed), no support for import formats other than the specified two-column CSV, no multi-user or profile switching. Each of cloud sync, shared decks, and marketplace must show up in the final output as an explicit named gap with a one-paragraph honest note on what real infrastructure it would need — not omitted, not stubbed with a disabled button that implies "coming soon."

On production-readiness: for this app "production-ready" cannot mean "compiles and the happy path demoes well." It means the SM-2 module has a passing test suite that specifically includes the four categories named above (first review, lapse reset, ease floor, day-boundary/timezone), the app has been actually run in the Simulator through a full create-deck → add-cards → review → check-stats → export-CSV → reimport loop, dark mode has been visually checked not just theoretically supported, and the force-quit-mid-session data-durability behavior has been manually verified, not assumed from architecture. If any of those verifications didn't happen, later phases need to say so honestly rather than mark the app done.

My decision rule for conflicts: where the prompt and the global playbook agree (never fake success states, no third-party SDKs, honest gaps), there's no ambiguity, follow both. Where the prompt is silent (widget, Siri, custom card templates, tags beyond decks), default to not building it — smaller finished app over larger half-built one, per the global rule — and log it as an explicit non-goal rather than silently deciding either way. Where "polished" (prompt) and "favor complete over broad" (prompt) could tempt scope expansion into things like themes, multiple card types, or LaTeX/markdown rendering in cards, resolve in favor of narrower and rock-solid: the six numbered core features, done completely, with the SM-2 engine bulletproof, beats seven features done adequately.

Numbered testable requirements extracted from the prompt, for later phases to check the shipped app against directly:

1. App launches and functions fully with the device/simulator in airplane mode; no feature silently fails or hangs waiting on network.
2. User can create a deck, edit its name, archive it, and archived decks no longer appear in the default review flow.
3. User can create a card with front, back, and optional note text inside a deck; can edit an existing card; editing supports keyboard-only flow (tab/return between fields, no forced mouse/tap-only interaction) with no unnecessary taps.
4. SM-2 scheduling module exists as an isolated, non-UI-coupled unit (no SwiftData/SwiftUI imports in the core algorithm) with unit tests proving: (a) a brand-new card's first Again/Hard/Good/Easy grade produces the correct initial interval and repetition count, (b) an Again grade after 1+ successful repetitions resets repetition count to 0 and interval to 1, (c) ease factor never drops below its floor regardless of how many consecutive Again grades occur, (d) a card's due-date comparison against "today" is computed using local calendar-day boundaries, verified correct across a simulated DST transition and across a review made just before vs. just after local midnight.
5. Starting a review session shows only cards due today (or earlier) for the selected deck or across all decks; a card with no due cards in the selected scope shows an honest empty state, not a blank screen.
6. Tapping a card reveals the back; grading with Again/Hard/Good/Easy immediately persists the new schedule for that card before advancing to the next card.
7. Force-quitting the app mid-session and relaunching shows all previously graded cards in this session already rescheduled correctly, and ungraded cards from that session still due.
8. Session-end summary displays accurate count of cards reviewed, again-rate (%), and elapsed time for that specific session.
9. Stats screen renders a 30-day due-forecast bar chart, a daily review-count history chart, and a retention rate (%Good+Easy out of graded) for both a single deck and "all decks" — and each chart shows a designed empty/sparse state (not a crash, not a blank chart) when there's under some threshold of data.
10. User can export a deck to a CSV file containing all its cards (front, back at minimum) via the standard iOS share sheet or files flow.
11. User can pick a two-column CSV to import, see a preview of what will be created before committing, and get a per-row error report for any malformed row rather than a silent skip or a generic failure message.
12. User can enable a daily local reminder notification and pick a time; if notification permission is denied, the UI reflects that truthfully rather than claiming the reminder is active.
13. Settings contains a "demo data" toggle; enabling it seeds two visibly-labeled demo decks with a plausible multi-week review history so stats charts show real-looking data; disabling it fully removes that seeded data rather than hiding it.
14. Cloud sync, shared/community decks, and a deck marketplace are each explicitly documented as a not-built gap with a short note on what real implementation would require, and no UI element in the shipped app implies any of them currently work.
